'They turned their faces toward the east, and stretching out their hands, they prayed together to God' — the eastward orientation in prayer is a FIXED EOTC LITURGICAL POSTURE (codified in Didascalia Apostolorum II.57, retained in Ethiopian practice). Parallels Daniel 6:10 (Daniel praying with windows opened toward Jerusalem). The Tewahedo Office (Säʿatat / Liturgy of the Hours) preserves eastward-prayer as the canonical posture for all liturgical prayer.

The brothers are physically formidable — bear-strangling + lion-killing-with-a-stone (2:9) + sword-felling-a-man-with-one-stroke (2:10) — feats reminiscent of SAMSON (Judges 14:5-6 lion-slaying) and DAVID'S MIGHTY MEN (2 Samuel 23:8-23). 'They were warriors of great strength; and they had comeliness, and the loveliness of speech. Moreover, the beauty of their outward appearance was wonderful; but because they worshiped God and did not fear death, the BEAUTY OF THEIR INWARD HEART SURPASSED ALL' (vv. 11-12). Contrastive-ethics anchor: outward-beauty + warrior-strength + eloquence are real-but-secondary virtues; the beauty-of-the-inward-heart (worship + fearlessness-of-death) is the SURPASSING VIRTUE. Parallels 1 Peter 3:3-4 (Petrine 'the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit' — patristically read by Augustine + Chrysostom as the canonical Christian inward-beauty anchor) + 1 Samuel 16:7 ('man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart'). The verse frames the brothers' subsequent martyrdom as the manifestation of inner-virtue under outward-suffering.

'Among them was one who would strangle a bear and kill it — he would choke it like a chicken on the spot' — WARRIOR-OF-MARTYRDOM motif distinctive to the Meqabyan trilogy. The brothers are physically formidable — bear-strangling + lion-killing-with-a-stone (2:9) + sword-felling-a-man-with-one-stroke (2:10) — feats reminiscent of SAMSON (Judges 14:5-6 lion-slaying) and DAVID'S MIGHTY MEN (2 Samuel 23:8-23). The composition stages a MARTYRDOM-OF-WARRIORS: men who COULD fight successfully but CHOOSE surrender to a higher commandment. Distinguishes Meqabyan from the standard LXX 2 Maccabees 7 passive-sufferer martyrology — the brothers' eventual surrender (2:27 + 3:1ff.) frames martyrdom as a freely-chosen offering of victory-capacity to God, not as a fight lost.

'They were warriors of great strength; and they had comeliness, and the loveliness of speech. Moreover, the beauty of their outward appearance was wonderful; but because they worshiped God and did not fear death, the BEAUTY OF THEIR INWARD HEART SURPASSED ALL' (vv. 11-12). Contrastive-ethics anchor: outward-beauty + warrior-strength + eloquence are real-but-secondary virtues; the beauty-of-the-inward-heart (worship + fearlessness-of-death) is the SURPASSING VIRTUE. Parallels 1 Peter 3:3-4 (Petrine 'the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit' — patristically read by Augustine + Chrysostom as the canonical Christian inward-beauty anchor) + 1 Samuel 16:7 ('man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart'). The verse frames the brothers' subsequent martyrdom as the manifestation of inner-virtue under outward-suffering.

'Unless you bring us those warriors — THE MEQABYANS — we will burn your city with fire' — THE EPONYM VERSE of the entire trilogy. The king's troops apply the collective designation መቃብያንን (the Meqabyans) to Maqabis-of-Benjamin's sons. From this naming the ENTIRE THREE-BOOK TRILOGY (1 Mq + 2 Mq + 3 Mq) takes its title. The Geʽez form, retained in the Amharic, is the source of all later renderings (Meqabyan, Maqabyan, Maccabean in popular English usage). Per Horovitz 1905 p. 195 fn. 3 + Dillmann Lexicon Linguae Aethiopicae (1865): etymology shows Seleucid-coin attestation under Antiochus IV — but the Ethiopian Meqabyan narrative is otherwise INDEPENDENT of the Greek Maccabees (Horovitz 'von Christus nirgends die Rede'; the books are distinctively Ethiopian in content).

'They turned their faces toward the east, and stretching out their hands, they prayed together to God' — the eastward orientation in prayer is a FIXED EOTC LITURGICAL POSTURE (codified in Didascalia Apostolorum II.57, retained in Ethiopian practice). Parallels Daniel 6:10 (Daniel praying with windows opened toward Jerusalem). The Tewahedo Office (Säʿatat / Liturgy of the Hours) preserves eastward-prayer as the canonical posture for all liturgical prayer.

'We have no desire to hear the word of that lawless man who does not believe in your law but trusts in GOLD AND SILVER, AND IN STONE AND WOOD MADE BY THE HAND OF MAN' — direct anti-idolatry creed echoing Psalm 115:4-7 LXX ('their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands... they have mouths and speak not... they have hands and handle not'); Psalm 135:15-18; Isaiah 44:9-20 (the long anti-idolatry-satire of carved-wood-worship); Wisdom of Solomon 13-15. The four-fold material-list (gold + silver + stone + wood) is the standard Hebrew-Bible idol-catalog; Meqabyan preserves it as the brothers' prayer-language. The verse functions as the brothers' grounds for refusal: idolatry as ontological-fraud (worship of made-things-by-the-hand-of-man) rather than as ritual-impurity.

'While You are the Creator who saves and who kills, he makes himself as though [the idols] had created him; HE IS ONE WHO SHEDS THE BLOOD OF MAN AND EATS THE FLESH OF MAN' — child-sacrifice intensifier. The phrase 'sheds the blood of man and eats the flesh of man' picks up the child-sacrifice motif from 1:14 (priests of Ṣiruṣaydan ate from defiled sacrifices) and intensifies it. The accusation is now placed in the mouth of the martyrs themselves as part of their GROUNDS FOR REFUSAL. Parallels the Hebrew-Bible polemic against Moloch / Molech child-sacrifice (Lev 18:21 + Lev 20:2-5 + 2 Kings 16:3 + 2 Kings 21:6 + Jeremiah 7:31 + Jeremiah 19:5 + Ezekiel 16:20-21) and the Wisdom of Solomon 14:23 polemic ('they slaughtered the children'). The Meqabyan placement in the martyrs' prayer locates the brothers' resistance theologically.
